lead: Spread spectrum takes a narrowband signal and deliberately spreads it over a much wider band using a fast pseudorandom code. The receiver knows the code and collapses the signal back, while interference stays spread. This gives resistance to jamming, hiding in noise, and multiple users in one band. DSSS multiplies data by a code; FHSS hops the carrier. GPS, Bluetooth and CDMA use these ideas.
prereq: You need: BPSK from 6.2 and noise and random processes from Unit 1.

sections.h3: PN code, chips and processing gain

blocks.text: A pseudorandom (PN) sequence is a binary sequence that looks random but repeats after a fixed length. A shift register with feedback generates it. In spread spectrum the PN sequence runs much faster than the data. Each PN bit is called a chip. One data bit is multiplied by many chips.
G_p = R_c / R_b    and    G_p(dB) = 10 log10(R_c / R_b)
blocks.where: G_p is the processing gain, unitless; R_c is the chip rate in chips per second; R_b is the data bit rate in bits per second; G_p(dB) is the processing gain in decibels.

blocks.text: G_p is the number of chips per data bit. A larger G_p spreads the signal wider, needs more bandwidth, and suppresses interference better. A PN code should have a sharp autocorrelation peak at zero shift and small cross-correlation with other codes.
Typical processing gains run from tens to thousands. The spreading does not change the data rate; it changes the bandwidth occupied and the receiver's ability to reject unwanted signals.
Direct-sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) multiplies the bipolar data d(t) by a PN code c(t). Both take values +1 and −1. The product d(t)c(t) is then BPSK modulated.
s(t) = A d(t) c(t) cos(2π f_c t)
blocks.where: s(t) is the transmitted signal; A is the carrier amplitude; d(t) is the bipolar data at bit rate R_b; c(t) is the PN code at chip rate R_c; f_c is the carrier frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: The receiver multiplies by the same carrier and the same code. Since c²(t)=1, the data bit returns. The receiver integrates over one bit period T_b and decides. The same code and chip timing are required; a wrong code gives near-zero correlation.

A narrowband jammer at the carrier frequency enters the receiver. Multiplication by c(t) spreads the jammer over R_c, so only about R_b/R_c = 1/G_p of its power falls in the data band. This is the processing gain. The jamming margin is the extra jammer power the link can tolerate.

blocks.where: M_j is the jamming margin in dB; G_p(dB) is the processing gain in dB; (E_b/N_0)_req is the required bit energy to noise density ratio in dB for the target error rate; losses are ignored.

blocks.text: Code acquisition finds the code phase. Tracking keeps chip alignment after acquisition.

Frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) keeps data modulation narrowband but changes the carrier frequency. A PN code drives a frequency synthesizer that selects one frequency from a hop set at each hop. The receiver uses the same hop pattern and synthesizer, so it follows the transmitter.
Slow hopping uses one hop for several data symbols. Fast hopping uses several hops within one symbol; the receiver must combine the hops coherently or noncoherently.

FHSS avoids a narrowband jammer because the carrier sits on any one frequency only briefly. A jammer must cover the whole hop band. DSSS spreads each symbol in frequency by the code; FHSS spreads over time by hopping the carrier.

CDMA multiple access lets many DSSS users share one band. Each user has a distinct PN code. The receiver correlates with one code; other users' signals have small cross-correlation and appear as noise. This is code-division multiple access. Capacity analysis is left to advanced courses.

figure.caption: The data is multiplied by the PN code before BPSK and multiplied by the same code after demodulation. The integrator adds one bit's worth of chips; the code and chip timing must match.

spec.title: DSSS transmitter and receiver
spec.aria: Data is multiplied by a PN code, BPSK modulated, sent through a channel, demodulated, multiplied again by the same PN code, integrated and thresholded.

examples.question: A DSSS link sends data at R_b = 9.6 kbps using a PN code at R_c = 1.2288 Mcps. (a) Find the processing gain as a ratio and in dB. (b) The required E_b/N_0 for the target bit error rate is 7 dB. Find the jamming margin in dB, ignoring losses.
examples.answer: The processing gain is 128, or about 21.07 dB; the jamming margin is about 14.07 dB.
examples.check:
import math
Rb = 9.6e3
Rc = 1.2288e6
Gp = Rc / Rb
Gp_dB = 10 * math.log10(Gp)
EbN0_dB = 7
Jm = Gp_dB - EbN0_dB
print(Gp)
print(round(Gp_dB, 2))
print(round(Jm, 2))

traps: Chip rate is not bit rate. R_c counts chips per second and is larger than R_b by the processing gain.
Processing gains add in dB. Do not add linear ratios and then convert unless you are multiplying them.
Jamming margin subtracts the required E_b/N_0 in dB: M_j = G_p(dB) − (E_b/N_0)_req. A common slip is to add them.
Despreading needs the same PN code and chip timing. A different code, or a code delayed by one chip, does not recover the data.
Slow and fast hopping differ by hops per symbol: slow has one hop per several symbols, fast has several hops per symbol.

quiz.q: What is a chip in spread spectrum?
quiz.a: A chip is one bit of the PN code. The PN code runs at chip rate R_c, which is higher than the data bit rate R_b.

quiz.q: Write the processing gain formula in linear and dB form.
quiz.a: G_p = R_c/R_b, unitless. G_p(dB) = 10 log10(R_c/R_b), where R_c is chip rate and R_b is bit rate.

quiz.q: Why does a narrowband jammer lose power in a DSSS receiver?
quiz.a: The receiver multiplies the incoming signal by the PN code. This spreads the narrowband jammer over the chip bandwidth. Only about 1/G_p of the jammer power remains in the data band after despreading.

quiz.q: A DSSS system has R_b = 20 kbps and R_c = 2.56 Mcps. Find G_p as a ratio and in dB.
A DSSS link has G_p = 21 dB and requires E_b/N_0 = 7 dB. Find the jamming margin in dB, ignoring losses.
The receiver PN code matches the transmitter code, but the chip clock is offset by half a chip. What happens to correlation and bit error rate?
quiz.a: The correlation peak is reduced, so the despread data amplitude falls and noise and interference grow relative to it. Bit error rate rises. Chip timing must be tracked closely after acquisition.

quiz.q: Compare slow and fast FHSS in receiver complexity and jam resistance.
quiz.a: Slow FHSS has one hop per several symbols, so the receiver stays on each frequency longer and is simpler. Fast FHSS has several hops per symbol, needs faster synchronization and combining, and is more resistant to a follower jammer.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern Wi-Fi uses OFDM, but spread-spectrum ideas remain in GPS, Bluetooth, CDMA cellular and LoRa chirp modulation. Ultra-wideband and military anti-jam radios use very large processing gain. Research topics include code design, synchronization and multi-user detection. Search for 'DSSS acquisition', 'frequency hopping synthesizer settling time' and 'CDMA near-far problem'.
